newsitem.title: USA: U.S., Mexico squash messy tomato fight.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Mexico squash messy tomato fight.

text.p: The U.S. Commerce Department said Friday it reached a tentative agreement with Mexican tomato growers to squash a bitter trade dispute.

The proposed agreement will settle a controversial complaint brought by Florida tomato growers against Mexican tomato producers for allegedly selling their produce in the United States at below-market prices and costing the domestic industry hundreds of millions of dollars in lost sales.

The tomato fight had threatened to explode into a potentially ugly and messy full-fledged trade war between the two neighbours and threaten commerce in a large variety of high-volume, high-priced products.

The dispute also stirred up charges that Florida growers have been seeking undue protection in an election year, and that because of Florida's 25 electoral votes, the Clinton administration has looked more sympathetically at the U.S. industry's complaint.

Under the proposed settlement, which was signed late Thursday by U.S. officials and Mexican growers, Mexican tomato growers would agree to not sell their produce in the United States at less than a so-called reference price of 20.68 cents per pound, or about $5.17 per 25-pound box.

This past winter, wholesale tomato prices dropped to $3 per box and even lower because of increased supplies and competition. The new minimum price can be adjusted after one year if market conditions change significantly.

Florida tomato growers hailed the agreement, which they said would establish a fair market and help get the industry back on its feet. They said it will not increase tomato prices for consumers, but in fact will result in a more stable market and more stable prices.
"We're very happy about this. This is something that works for both sides," said Ray Gilmer of the Florida Fruit & Vegetable Association.
"This pact helps ensure ... competitive pricing for consumers," said Mike Stuart of the Florida group.
Commerce Secretary Mickey Kantor said the agreement "will provide strong relief to tomato growers in Florida and other states and help preserve jobs in the industry."

Agriculture Department Secretary Dan Glickman said he was pleased with the agreement and said it showed that U.S. trade laws can protect U.S. industries from unfair competition "without unduly restricting trade and adversely impacting consumers."

Under the five-year agreement, which becomes official on Oct. 25, the U.S. government will implement a monitoring system for Mexican imports. The administration can terminate the pact at any time if it finds the terms have been violated.
The U.S. side hopes the pact will remove a political thorn in the side of the Clinton administration, which appeared to have backed itself into a no-win situation.
Consumer advocates and major agricultural groups representing big-ticket items like feedgrains and livestock have strongly opposed the industry's complaint.

They have charged that the Florida growers were seeking unwarranted protection and that tomato prices would rise and trade with Mexico suffer if the administration slapped sanctions on Mexican imports.

Some critics of the complaint have blamed Florida's practice of picking tomatoes green and then artificially ripening them for the decreased demand. Mexico normally ships vine-ripened tomatoes, which many consumers say are tastier.
Florida growers strongly defend their product.

"We're confident that we can compete with anything Mexico produces, vine-ripened or not, as long as there is fair pricing going on," said Gilmer. "Florida produces some of best-tasting tomatoes in the world."
